Very Strange Experience:

They’ve brought a new person to this Masjid and he has some very strange things with him that are astonishing for anyone who has basic understanding of Islam. Yesterday at the Khutbah I only heard the last 10 minutes of it, and all of these blunders were heard from him:

1. The Khateeb quoted an Ayah, and then quoted Tony Robinson (a non muslim) and said “He is making tafseer of such and such ayah” …… what? Why not quote the Tafsir of Ibn Kathīr, Tafsir of Tabari, Or other than them? I mean, that is extremely strange for anyone who has studied Islam under Sunni scholars (not sufis) He seems to try to relate to the audience and make things very modernistic and humorous, meanwhile the glory of honor of Islam lies in returning to how things were originally.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

«إن طول صلاة الرجل وقصر خطبته مئنة من فقهه»
“Indeed, the length of a man’s prayer and the brevity of his khutbah are an indication of his understanding.

(Instead the Khateeb prolongs the Khutbah and shortens the prayer)

Ibn Mas'ud رضي الله انه said:

"Learn knowledge before it is taken away, and it is taken away by the death of the scholars. Beware of going to extremes and delving too deeply, and beware of bid’ah (religious innovations). Upon you is to adhere to the ancient affair."

Jami Bayān Al-'Ilm wa Fadlihī 1/152

2. The Khateeb has excessive humor and jokes, half the khutbah feels like satire. This conflicts with the necessary rujoolah (manhood) required in the religion and he tries too hard to relate to the audience especially the youth. He goes on a lot of tangents and side discussions, seems to be a flatterer (mudaahin) wants the people to like him a lot, maybe to bring them close to teach them his strange ideologies and ways of thinking. This is immature and a leader in the community should be someone who is upright, upon seriousness, but at the same time well mannered and humble to the people, not harsh. He was talking about creme rolls and sweet custard and other strange things. The behavior of the Prophet ﷺ wasn’t clownish. I personally do not see him fit to be a leader or khateeb. The Sahaba mentioned those who constantly indulge in levity and entertainment and story telling are not in
reality people of knowledge.

Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh رضي الله عنهما said:

كان رسول الله ﷺ إذا خطب احمرت عيناه، وعلا صوته، واشتد غضبه، حتى كأنه منذر جيش يقول: صبحكم ومساكم

“Whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a khutbah, his eyes would become red, his voice would become raised, and his anger would become intense, as though he were warning an army…”

Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

3. He says the best thing in Jannah is the company of the Prophet ﷺ and Sahaabah. Rather the scholars of Ahlus Sunnah affirmed the best thing in Jannah is seeing the face of Allah as it has come in the Qur’an & hadith. And we do not say Allah’s face is like the creation, ask why or how it is, or giving it interpretations from greek philosophy and mantiq. We affirm it how it comes just as the Salaf did.

1. Sūrah al-Qiyāmah 75:22–23

وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ ۝ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ

“Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.”

The Prophet ﷺ said:

إنكم سترون ربكم كما ترون القمر ليلة البدر، لا تضامون في رؤيته

“You will certainly see your Lord just as you see the full moon, and you will not be harmed or inconvenienced in seeing Him.”

Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

4. He Speaks more about the Prophet ﷺ than he speaks about Allah سبحانه وتعالى. This is no surprise coming from a Sufi, some of them practically worship the Prophet ﷺ
As the Christians worship ‘Isa عليه السلام.

And he ﷺ said:

«لا تطروني كما أطرت النصارى ابن مريم»
“Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising the son of Mary.”
— Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī

Overall we do not see this person fitting to be a leader and he should be replaced with a person who is a caller to Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ upon the understanding of the First Three Generations. It is very sad what the community has stooped down
towards in terms of standards.

reviews.name: Aqeedah Ahlus Sunnah
reviews.text:
**Beware**

Masjid Tawheed Brings Sufis to Give Khutub on Jum’ah and to Teach

I was disturbed to hear today in the Khutbah the following:

- The Khateeb stated the Incorrect Definition of “La illaha illa Allah”
It does not mean  “There is no God but Allah” even the Quraysh Affirmed that Meaning. “There is no creator except Allah”.” That is not the intended meaning. The correct meaning is “There is no deity worthy of worship in truth except Allah.” Therefore; Dua, Salah, sacrifice, taking oaths, and all acts of worship are directed to Allah alone. This is from the Clear Matters. The Prophet ﷺ after his death is no longer a Waseelah. We cannot ask him for our needs. Nor can we Ask Allah “By the Honor of your Prophet ﷺ” this is Innovation. The Companions sought Waseelah from the Prophet ﷺ while he was ALIVE. Not after his death.

The scholars defined Legitimate Waseelah or Tawassul as:

- Tawassul through Allah’s Names and Attributes.
- Tawassul through one’s righteous deeds.
- Asking a LIVING righteous person to make duʿāʾ for you.

- The Khateeb stated the Prophet ﷺ is Alive. This is deceptive and misleading. He is dead in this World, but Alive in the Barzakh, when we send salawat, it goes to him in the Barzakh. He does not see or know what is happening in the World currently. Many Sufis use this “He is alive” to mislead people into Asking the Prophet ﷺ in Dua for their Needs which is Major Shirk.

“Yā Muḥammad, cure me.”
“Yā Rasūlallāh, forgive my sin.”
“Yā Rasūlallāh, rescue me.”

This is duʿāʾ Dua is Worship, and Dua directed toward other than Allah when the person is asking him for something that only Allah can provide. This is Major Shirk. Many Muslims fall into this today.

And Allah commands:

إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ

“You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.”

Shaykh Ibn Bāz رحمه الله explicitly says:

دعاء الميت والاستغاثة به فذلك من الشرك الأكبر

“Calling upon the dead and seeking their aid is major shirk.”

- The Khateeb then brings the Argument

“It is only shirk if the person believes the one he is calling upon is Allah”

So the pagan Arabs in the Prophet’s time ﷺ did not believe their idols were Allah. They distinguished between Allah and the objects they worshipped. They said “these are our intercessors”

Yet Allah still judged their worship of other than Him to be shirk.

Allah quotes them:

ما نعبدهم الا ليقربونا الى الله زلفى

“We only worship them so that they may bring us closer to Allah.”
Qur’an 39:3

Look at the argument carefully.

They did not say:

“These idols are Allah.”

Rather, they said:

“We worship them because they bring us closer to Allah.”

So their fundamental problem (the pagan arabs) was not that they believed their idols were Allah. These sufis like the Khateeb today, taint the Aqeedah of the Muslims and misguide them. However there are knowledgeable people in the community who know better and will refute them seeking the face and pleasure of Allah.

Suppose somebody says:

“I don’t believe Muhammad ﷺ is Allah. I know Allah is the Creator. I only call upon Muhammad ﷺ to bring me closer to Allah and to intercede for me.”

That argument does not establish Tawhid.

It is essentially the same justification Allah quoted from the pagans:

ما نعبدهم الا ليقربونا الى الله زلفى

“We only worship them so that they may bring us closer to Allah.”

—

Reading the Prophet’s ﷺ Sīrah is unquestionably something good. We should study his life throughout the entire year.

The issue is when someone specifically establishes:

“Rabīʿ al-Awwal is the month in which we should gather and commemorate the Prophet’s birth.”

and makes this an annual religious observance.

There is no authentic evidence that the Companions, Tābiʿūn, or the early generations established an annual Mawlid.

Historically, the earliest documented institutional celebrations of the Prophet’s birthday are associated with the Fāṭimid Ismāʿīlī Shiʿi dynasty in Egypt.

—

Lastly This is “Masjid Tawheed” but they bring people who teach Shirk and destroy the hereafter of the people. May Allah guide us.

reviews.name: Omar A
reviews.text:
Bukhl (stinginess) is especially blameworthy when it prevents the proper maintenance of the houses of Allah. A masjid collects donations regularly, has membership subscriptions, yet basic needs such as a working speaker system that allows the congregation to hear the imām, remains neglected. The audio quality is extremely poor, and it cuts out for minutes straight while worshippers in the outside overflow are confused about whether they should be in Ruku or Sujud or if the Prayer is still going on.

Wealth entrusted to a masjid is an amānah. It should be spent wisely on what serves the worship of Allah and benefits the Muslims, not withheld while obvious deficiencies remain.

The administrators of masjid tawheed in elk grove should ask themselves:

Would I accept this level of neglect if it were my own home?

So how about the House of Allah?

۞ أَتَأْمُرُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ بِٱلْبِرِّ وَتَنسَوْنَ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ تَتْلُونَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ ۚ أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ ٤٤

Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture?* Do you not understand?
reviews.responseFromOwnerText:
Dear Omar, Thank you for taking the time to share your concerns. We sincerely appreciate feedback from our community, as it helps us improve the experience for everyone.

Regarding the sound system, we have reached out to several professional audio companies to evaluate our current setup and recommend improvements especially for outdoors. We also want to note that we did not receive any reports today or during previous Jumu’ahs of the audio cutting out completely. It’s possible there was a localized issue with one of the outdoor speakers or wiring. We will be checking the outdoor system tonight to ensure everything is functioning properly.

Alhamdulillah, Masjid Al-Tawheed is committed to financial transparency. We post our monthly profit and loss statements in the masjid hallway, provide detailed financial reports to our members, and conduct an annual financial summary open to all of the community. 

If you have experience with audio systems or would like to volunteer, recommend a company, or share resources that could help improve the system, we would sincerely welcome your assistance. Please feel free to contact the masjid directly at 916-686-9519 or stop by the office. Our doors are always open, and we value constructive input from our community.

May Allah reward everyone who sincerely strives to improve His House and reward our volunteers for their efforts. Ameen.

reviews.responseFromOwnerText:
Thank you for taking the time to share your feedback. We are truly sorry to hear about your past experiences and will continue working to ensure everyone feels welcome in our community.
We would like to share that our masjid is actually the only one in the Bay Area with a full-time lady scholar on site, dedicated to serving our sisters’ spiritual and educational needs. We have recently renovated a brand-new women’s space to provide a more comfortable and welcoming environment, and we regularly host women’s-only programs that address modern-day issues and contemporary topics.

Our masjid is also one of the most diverse in San Francisco, bringing together members from many cultures and backgrounds. Over the years, we have hosted numerous events to engage with our neighbors and city officials, building strong community ties.

To ensure each visitor receives the proper attention and time, we recommend booking an appointment to meet with our scholars, as we typically do not offer drop-in consultations unless it is an emergency. Please also note that our doors are often locked in the evenings as an added layer of security for the safety of the girls and women inside the masjid.

If you would like to connect directly, please visit: https://www.icofsf.org/contact-1. We hope you will give us another opportunity to welcome you warmly and personally.

reviews.text:
For my school project, I visited a mosque in my community. I chose the Dinuba Mosque because I had never been inside a mosque before and I was curious about what it would be like. At first, I was a little nervous because I didn’t know what to expect. Before going, I looked up what I needed to do as a woman visiting a mosque. I learned that I should cover my hair and wear appropriate clothing, which I completely understood and respected since it’s important in their religion.

When I arrived, everyone I met was very friendly and welcoming. They made me feel comfortable right away, which helped ease my nerves. I had to ask questions and conduct an interview for my project, and everyone was very kind and willing to help. They answered my questions and explained things clearly.

During my visit, I learned about why Muslims pray five times a day and the importance of prayer in their daily lives. It was interesting to hear how prayer helps them stay connected to their faith and gives them time throughout the day to reflect and focus.

Overall, my visit to the Dinuba Mosque was an amazing experience. Even though I was nervous at first, the welcoming environment and friendly people made it a great learning opportunity. I’m really glad I chose to visit the mosque for my project.

reviews.name: IFIqbal
reviews.text:
I had the opportunity to attend the Muharram majalis here again this year, and I can honestly say my experience was just as welcoming and uplifting as it was last year.

One of the most meaningful improvements I noticed was how the Resident Scholar, Sheikh Ahmad Modarres, emphasized not only the timeless lessons of Karbala but also the importance of remembering our Muslim brothers and sisters around the world who are facing oppression, conflict, hardship, and poverty. It was heartening to see charitable initiatives highlighted during the program, encouraging the community to support those in need. As someone who mentioned this in my previous review, it was truly meaningful to see that message reflected this year.

Despite the large crowds on the 9th and 10th of Muharram, the organization was outstanding. The volunteers and community members remained calm, respectful, patient, and welcoming throughout the evening. I especially appreciated the inclusive atmosphere and the diversity of cultures and ethnic backgrounds represented within the congregation, creating a genuine sense of unity and belonging.

Sheikh Ahmad Modarres delivered thoughtful, well-structured, and intellectually engaging lectures each evening. Every topic was presented with clarity and then beautifully connected to the timeless message of Karbala. His delivery was sincere, compassionate, and respectful—never theatrical or excessive. His recitation of the noha and masaib was heartfelt, dignified, and emotionally moving, while maintaining the reverence these sacred gatherings deserve.

The overall decorum of the majlis reflected excellent organization and respect. The congregation remained attentive, the environment was peaceful, and there was a clear sense of purpose throughout the programs. The dedication of the organizers and volunteers was evident in every detail.

Overall, this mosque continues to provide a meaningful, inclusive, and spiritually enriching Muharram experience. I am grateful for the warmth, hospitality, and dedication shown by the community, and I look forward to attending again, Insha’Allah.

The current board is made up of multiple family members, which creates a clear conflict of interest and raises serious concerns about how the donations are being managed.

A masjid’s funds should always be public and transparent. If you wish to donate, I strongly advise you to ask the board to openly show where the funds have gone and provide a clear record of donations over the last several years.

I was homeless at the time, and I had nowhere to shower, pray, or perform wudu. If I remember correctly, I had been coming to this mosque for about a week because I needed a safe place to pray and perform wudu.

One day, I went into the women’s restroom to perform wudu before prayer. I was partially undressed, as you normally have to be when performing wudu. Suddenly, a male security guard opened the door and walked into the women’s restroom.

He told me that this place was “not for homeless people.” I explained to him that I was there to pray and perform wudu. I also asked him why he was entering the women’s restroom while I was inside. Instead of leaving, he started yelling at me and continued standing inside the women’s restroom.

I was already going through an extremely difficult period in my life, and this experience left me devastated. I was crying when I went into the mosque to pray. The women’s prayer area was closed at the time, so I went into the main hall.

While I was there, I heard the security guard speaking with the imam. He was telling the imam that he had done the right thing by opening the door and entering the women’s restroom. From what I heard, the guard had assumed that I was homeless and that I was coming to the mosque simply to shower.

Being treated that way in a place where I came seeking peace, prayer, and safety was deeply hurtful and humiliating. I understand that a mosque may have rules regarding its facilities, but there are respectful ways to communicate those rules without yelling at someone or entering a women’s restroom while she is partially undressed.

You can decide for yourself whether you want to visit this mosque. Personally, after this experience, I will never return.

reviews.text:
I attended the Khatm program on Laylatul Qadr for the first time, and unfortunately the experience was very disappointing. This night is one of the most spiritually important nights for Muslims, a time when people come to the mosque to pray, reflect, and strengthen their connection with Allah. I was really looking forward to a meaningful and uplifting gathering.
However, most of the time was spent talking about how much money the mosque needs and asking for donations. While I understand that mosques require financial support to operate, Laylatul Qadr should primarily be focused on worship, prayer, and reminding people of the spiritual value and blessings of the night.
As a first-time attendee of Khatm, I expected to hear more about the significance of the night, the rewards of prayer and supplication, and guidance on how to benefit from such a special occasion. Instead, the constant focus on fundraising made the atmosphere feel less spiritual and, honestly, quite boring. I say this with respect and sincerity: I hope in the future the program can focus more on worship, reflection, and the spiritual importance of Laylatul Qadr. Many people attend on this night seeking peace, inspiration, and closeness to Allah, and it would be wonderful if the program reflected that purpose more clearly

The Fullerton Muslim
Community Center (FMCC) is an absolute gem in North Orange County. From the moment you walk in, you feel a genuine sense of warmth and belonging. The facility is well-maintained, clean, and provides a peaceful environment for worship. It's also inspiring to see their rich history as a foundation for the local Cham Muslim community while remaining beautifully inclusive to Muslims of all backgrounds. They offer great programs, youth activities, and weekly lectures that truly enrich the soul. If you're looking for a tight-knit, supportive, and spiritually uplifting spiritual home in the Fullerton area, I highly recommend visiting FMCC.

This is one of the best mosques I have ever visited in the United States; in fact, I can say it is unparalleled. The moment you enter the North Marin Mosque, you are enveloped in a sense of tranquility and peace rarely found elsewhere.

reviews.text:
A place that doesn't welcome children. My six-year-old daughter was fasting for the first time as an experiment, and she was excited to break her fast at the mosque today to experience the vibes of a Muslim family, the Islamic spirit of Ramadan, and the genuine feelings of fellow fasting Muslims, as we had recently moved to California. It was a new experience, and it was supposed to be a happy one. But what happened was the opposite. Today, Friday, February 27, 2026, I came to break my fast at the mosque with two children, one of whom was fasting. One of the volunteers gave me one meal and ignored me when I asked for meals for my children. My son and daughter then went to ask the volunteer, who ignored them, and then sat next to me waiting. I stayed waiting, not touching my meal, waiting for my children to start eating. Then they didn't bring any more meals. I encouraged both children to go and ask the volunteer, who was already distributing new meals. My daughter asked him if she could have some, and the man replied that he would bring some boxes inside. When the woman came inside with additional boxes, she ignored my children, who were following her and asking if they could have one. But this woman I ignored them too. Are we homeless? Are we begging for charity? Can't a holy place like a mosque preserve human dignity?

To those who occupy this place, if you don't welcome children, just say: Feed your children at home before coming to the mosque. There isn't enough food، or don’t bring your kids to the mosque!!!!

The mosque is the House of ALLAH.
I drove 25 minutes to get here and participate in this Iftar, to support the small mosque, and to experience the spirit of Muslims and the spirit of community. I was very excited about the activities and celebrations of Islamic occasions. How do you expect me to teach children to love the mosque and love the religion when you are driving them away? What was I supposed to tell my children when they asked me why they weren't given food?

In the end, I ended up giving my meal to my children and going hungry until after the Taraweeh prayer. I will never come back here, and I will never go to any mosque for Iftar during Ramadan.

I am angry, frustrated, and very upset.
